processing: The green tea is withered, fixed, rolled, baked, shaped, brought to show its down and dried. It comes as queshe, maofeng, maojian and chaoqing, and the name also covers other tea classes.
harvest_season: Picking opens when each square metre of the bush surface carries 10 to 15 standard buds, on clear mornings; as with other Sichuan greens, spring is the prized season.
appearance_dry: Flat, fairly even and straight, emerald green with some gloss.
taste_profile: Mellow and full with a fairly rich aroma; top grades carry an orchid note.

brewing.notes: General advice for Chinese greens. Queshe and maofeng grades want the cooler end; plain chaoqing takes hotter water.

vintage_note: Graded rather than aged: queshe, maofeng and maojian each come in four grades and chaoqing in five. As with other Chinese greens, it is sold from the current year's harvest, and spring lots of the higher grades are the ones to seek out.
description:
Wanyuan selenium tea comes from Wanyuan in the far northeast of Sichuan, in the Daba Mountains where the province meets Shaanxi and Chongqing. The name advertises the selenium in the area's soils, and that is really the frame around an otherwise classic mountain green.

Producers make several styles under the name. The green is sorted into queshe, maofeng, maojian and chaoqing, and the same growers can make all six classes of tea. Bashan Queshe is the best-known product in this family.

Good green lots are flat and glossy, with a mellow body and a yellow-green cup, and top grades have an orchid aroma. Brew by style: cooler for tender grades, hotter for the plain chaoqing.

The protected zone covers 112 villages in 48 townships. Choose by style, grade and harvest rather than the selenium claim, since the label's health language tells you nothing about how the tea tastes.
history:
Wanyuan is described as an old tea district, though specifics before the modern period are thin. Its modern record starts with awards at a national science and technology fair in 1991 and at the China International Agricultural Fair in 1999.

The Ministry of Agriculture registered the name as a geographical indication on 8 March 2010. It joined the ministry's national directory of notable agricultural products in 2015, and the city has taken on the title of China's selenium tea capital.
